summary: This RFC proposes a protocol that returns the user identification for a TCP connection. It is the second draft, superseding RFC 912, with a more formal syntax for requests and responses and a specified identification type. It was replaced by RFC 1413.

eli5.summary: A server answers, "Who owns this connection?" This second draft cleaned up how the question and answer are written.

questions: what is the authentication server protocol
subtitle: A protocol to identify the user behind a TCP connection.

tldr.problem: When a server receives a connection, it has no standard way to know who is using it. Applications needed a way to query for the owner of a TCP connection.
tldr.mechanism: The Authentication Server listens on TCP port 113 and answers simple queries: given a pair of port numbers (local and foreign), it returns the operating system type and user identifier of the connection owner on that host.
tldr.outcome: Applications could verify user identity automatically without a second login, or audit who is connected. This protocol (also called IDENT) became standard for such queries. RFC 1413 replaced it later.

today: RFC 931 defined the authentication server protocol, later standardized as the Ident Protocol. RFC 1413 replaced it with a refined version that is still referenced in authentication systems.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: The Authentication Server Protocol determines the identity of a user on a TCP connection. A server listens on TCP port 113 for queries. Given the port numbers of an established connection, the server returns the username and operating system type on the server's machine. This is the second draft, updated from RFC 912 with a more formal syntax for requests and responses.
sections.eli5: A server on port 113 answers the question: 'Who owns this connection?'

sections.title: Query and Response Format
sections.content: A client sends a simple query: two decimal port numbers separated by a comma (the local port on the target system and the foreign port on the source system), for example 23, 6191. The server responds with the same port pair, followed by either USERID or ERROR, and additional information. A successful response lists the operating system name (like MULTICS, TAC, UNIX) and the user identifier in that system's format. An error response explains why the user could not be identified: INVALID-PORT, NO-USER, or UNKNOWN-ERROR.
sections.eli5: You ask 'What's on port 23 and port 6191?', and it answers 'USERID : MULTICS : StJohns'.

sections.title: Uses and Restrictions
sections.content: Applications include automatic FTP authentication (skipping the login prompt), verification for privileged network operations, and eliminating double login for TELNET users. A critical restriction: a user on Host A can only query the authentication server on Host B about connections between A and B. This prevents unauthorized snooping. The RFC notes that trustworthiness varies by host, and applications must decide how much trust to place in returned information, possibly restricting use to locally controlled subnets.
sections.eli5: Servers can use this to auto-identify users, but you can only ask about your own connections to prevent spying.
